Refining rsa_l2_singleton by incorporating competitor confusion avoidance from competitor_confusion_speaker: Speakers evaluate candidate words not only by their informativeness to simulated listeners, but also by penalizing words that overlap with visually similar competitor objects in the context. This improves fit on displays where distractors share visual features with the intended referent, guiding listeners away from targets whose competitors create visual confusion. Differences from rsa_l2_singleton: - Recursion depth: Unchanged at depth 2 (choice_probs calls L2). - Parameters added: w_confusion (Normal(0.0, 1.0), penalizing candidate words proportional to their visual similarity overlap with alternative referents satisfying the word). - Parameters removed: None. - Other terms: Added compute_confusion to calculate pairwise visual similarity between referents and competitors sharing each utterance; incorporated - w_confusion * at(confusion, u, r) into the simulated speaker utility at both depth-1 (S1 in L1) and depth-2 (S2 in L2).

name: expressibility_prior_listener
detail: elpd_diff 74.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 20.4 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions by reasoning that speakers choose what to talk about based on an object's communicative expressibility—how uniquely and informatively that object can be identified in the scene. Rather than assuming speakers choose referents uniformly, listeners model a speaker who selects intended referents in proportion to their maximum recovery probability under the available vocabulary, favoring uniquely nameable objects over ambiguous or featureless items. On uninformative trials with no descriptive word, choices directly reflect this communicative expressibility expectation alongside visual singleton salience.

name: contextual_alignment_listener
detail: elpd_diff 75.6 > 2.0 x clustered dse 22.9 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions under uncertainty about which visual feature a word picks out, reasoning that an utterance can be associated with features that contextually co-occur with the named property across objects in the display. When interpreting a word, pragmatic listeners model a speaker who selects an informative feature to describe the intended referent and transmits that feature through this contextual alignment mapping, inverting the joint process to infer the referent. On uninformative trials with no descriptive word, choices default to common-ground visual singleton salience.

name: dilemma_fallback_speaker
detail: elpd_diff 79.8 > 2.0 x clustered dse 19.4 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: When an intended referent can be uniquely named in the display, speakers reliably produce that distinguishing descriptor to ensure communicative recovery. When an intended referent cannot be uniquely named, the speaker faces an expressive dilemma where no word guarantees recovery and falls back on selecting among imperfect descriptors with a distinct dilemma choice rationality. Pragmatic listeners invert this two-regime speaker, recognizing that ambiguous expressions indicate unnameable referents facing communicative compromise rather than uniquely nameable referents whose distinguishing descriptors were withheld.

name: bounded_sampling_listener
detail: elpd_diff 73.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 23.6 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions through resource-bounded sampled inference rather than exact Bayesian marginalization. When hearing a descriptive word, the listener draws a bounded budget of mental simulation samples from candidate referents in the visual scene, accepting an interpretation if the speaker would produce the heard expression. When the sample budget is exhausted without confirming an intended target, the listener defaults to visual prior expectations favoring unique singletons.

name: incremental_alternative_speaker
detail: elpd_diff 56.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 17.9 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Speakers formulate referring expressions by evaluating candidate words against an active alternative feature of the intended referent, choosing words that eliminate visual competitors the alternative feature left confusable. Pragmatic listeners invert this two-stage communicative process by jointly inferring the intended referent and the alternative descriptor the speaker sought to improve upon. On uninformative trials with no descriptive word, choices default to common-ground visual singleton salience.

name: aspect_goal_listener
detail: elpd_diff 66.1 > 2.0 x clustered dse 20.7 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions by reasoning about the speaker's communicative goal or question under discussion: rather than attempting to uniquely pinpoint the referent's complete scene identity, speakers aim to be informative about a specific visual aspect (feature) of the target object. When selecting which aspect of a referent to communicate, speakers favor features that are contextually informative and distinctive in the display, and express that chosen aspect with a descriptive word. Pragmatic listeners invert this process by jointly inferring the intended referent and the speaker's communicative goal, expecting a heard feature to pick out objects for which that feature was the most contextually relevant aspect to highlight.

name: diagnostic_evidence_listener
detail: elpd_diff 95.5 > 2.0 x clustered dse 27.6 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions by evaluating the weight of evidence each word provides in favor of the target over the scene distractors. Rather than engaging in nested recursive Theory of Mind, listeners invert a speaker who chooses descriptions proportional to their diagnostic log-odds—the degree to which the named feature singles out the intended referent rather than alternative objects in the context. On uninformative trials without a distinguishing word, choices default to visual singleton salience, favoring contextually unique objects over duplicated items.

name: exclusive_alternative_speaker
detail: elpd_diff 106.9 > 2.0 x clustered dse 30.9 vs rsa_l2_singleton_confusion_omission_cost (grouped CV on auto_psych trials)
hypothesis: Speakers formulate referring expressions by prioritizing dedicated exclusive descriptors that uniquely single out the target, penalizing ambiguous descriptors whenever the intended referent possesses a foolproof exclusive alternative in the display. Pragmatic listeners invert this speaker by directing ambiguous expressions toward candidate referents that lack any exclusive descriptor in the context. On a display where one candidate possesses an exclusive unique descriptor alongside the heard word while another candidate has multiple cluttered background features that are never exclusive, this exclusive-alternative listener selects the cluttered candidate because it lacked an exclusive descriptor, whereas the current best model selects the candidate with the exclusive descriptor due to accumulated omission and confusion penalties.
